title: Acute Pyelonephritis
bottomLine: Fever plus flank pain is an upper-UTI pattern; hypotension, confusion, oliguria, or obstruction turns it into an urgent sepsis/source-control problem. Obtain cultures when ordered without delaying urgent antimicrobials in a sick client.
recognize: Fever or rigors with flank/CVA pain
Dysuria may be present but is not required
Older adults may present with delirium or functional decline
Pregnancy and obstruction increase complication risk
differentiate: Cystitis usually lacks flank pain and systemic illness
Renal colic can cause severe flank pain but fever suggests infection
Glomerular disease is more likely with edema, hypertension, and glomerular hematuria/proteinuria
assessment: ABCs, perfusion, mental status, temperature, pain
workup: Imaging when obstruction, abscess, or treatment failure is suspected
management: Treat pain, fever, and nausea safely
Reassess culture results and clinical response
medicationSafety: Antibiotic choice must reflect allergy, pregnancy, renal function, culture, and local resistance
Renally cleared drugs may require adjustment in kidney injury
counselling: Seek urgent care for worsening fever, vomiting, reduced urine, or weakness/confusion
followUp: Review culture-directed therapy and renal function when indicated
examTrap: Treating fever plus obstruction as an uncomplicated UTI or delaying escalation because dysuria is absent.
oneLinePearl: Flank pain + fever = think upper UTI; obstruction + infection = emergency.

title: Nephrolithiasis and Renal Colic
bottomLine: Renal colic is usually severe, wave-like flank pain with nausea and possible hematuria. Fever, anuria, renal deterioration, or a solitary obstructed kidney changes the problem from painful to potentially life-threatening.
recognize: Colicky flank pain radiating toward groin
Pain can migrate as the stone moves
differentiate: Pyelonephritis adds fever/systemic illness
AAA or other vascular catastrophe must be considered in older/high-risk clients with sudden severe pain
Musculoskeletal pain is generally less colicky and lacks urinary findings
management: Hydrate appropriately rather than force fluids
medicationSafety: NSAIDs require renal, GI, pregnancy, and bleeding-risk review
Alpha-blockers can cause hypotension and are not universal for every stone
counselling: Hydration and prevention advice depend on stone type and comorbidities
Return urgently for fever, inability to urinate, or uncontrolled symptoms
followUp: Confirm stone passage or planned urology follow-up
Review stone analysis/metabolic prevention when appropriate
examTrap: Giving reassurance because the pain looks like a stone while missing fever and obstruction.
oneLinePearl: A stone hurts; an infected obstructed stone can kill.

title: Acute Glomerulonephritic Syndrome
bottomLine: Think inflamed glomeruli when dark urine, edema, hypertension, oliguria, and rising creatinine cluster together. The nursing danger is not the urine colour—it is filtration failure causing severe hypertension, hyperkalemia, or pulmonary edema.
differentiate: Lower UTI causes dysuria but not a classic edema/hypertension syndrome
Nephrotic syndrome has heavier protein loss/edema with less prominent inflammatory hematuria
Stone disease causes colic rather than a diffuse glomerular pattern
workup: CBC and disease-specific serology/complement when ordered
management: Control volume and BP as prescribed
Escalate pulmonary edema, severe hypertension, hyperkalemia
medicationSafety: Diuretics/antihypertensives require BP and renal monitoring
Avoid assuming nephrotoxic medication is safe during AKI
counselling: Report dyspnea, marked swelling, reduced urine, or severe headache promptly
followUp: Trend renal function, BP, urine findings, and edema
examTrap: Focusing on hematuria while missing volume overload and dangerous BP/electrolyte changes.
oneLinePearl: Dark urine gets attention; BP, lungs, potassium, and urine output determine danger.

title: Hydronephrosis and Obstructive Uropathy
bottomLine: Hydronephrosis means urine cannot drain normally. Infected obstruction, anuria, rising creatinine, or a blocked/dislodged drainage device requires rapid escalation because medication alone cannot fix a mechanical blockage.
recognize: Bladder distention when obstruction is lower
Renal dysfunction can be silent early
differentiate: Prerenal AKI has poor perfusion without a mechanical drainage problem
Stable chronic lymphedema/edema does not explain absent urinary drainage
Pyelonephritis can coexist and becomes especially dangerous with obstruction
workup: Bladder scan when lower obstruction is suspected
management: Monitor post-decompression urine and renal response
medicationSafety: Antibiotics do not replace drainage in infected complete obstruction
Do not manipulate/flush nephrostomy tubes outside authorized protocol
counselling: Protect drainage tubing and secure devices
Seek urgent help for fever, no drainage, worsening pain, or leakage/dislodgement
followUp: Verify restored output and renal recovery
Ensure urology/interventional follow-up for the cause
examTrap: Treating a blocked infected system with antibiotics alone while ignoring the need for drainage.
oneLinePearl: Obstruction is a plumbing problem—restore flow, especially when infection is present.

title: Autosomal Dominant Polycystic Kidney Disease
bottomLine: ADPKD is inherited progressive cystic kidney disease. Nursing priorities are BP control, renal surveillance, stone/infection recognition, adherence, and never dismissing sudden severe neurologic symptoms as 'just kidney disease.'
differentiate: Simple renal cysts do not create the same inherited multisystem pattern
Acute obstruction causes abrupt drainage problems rather than chronic bilateral cyst burden
management: Specialist-directed disease-modifying therapy in selected patients
medicationSafety: Renal function affects many drug doses
Pregnancy status can change antihypertensive and disease-modifying choices
counselling: Discuss inheritance and family screening with the care team
examTrap: Treating family history as incidental or delaying emergency assessment of a sudden neurologic event.
oneLinePearl: ADPKD is inherited kidney disease—control BP, protect kidneys, respect sudden neurologic red flags.

title: Placental Abruption
bottomLine: Painful bleeding, uterine tenderness/rigidity, and fetal compromise suggest placental abruption. Visible blood can underestimate hemorrhage because bleeding may be concealed; treat maternal shock and fetal deterioration as emergencies.
recognize: Vaginal bleeding may be small or absent
differentiate: Placenta previa classically causes painless bleeding
Labour pain is patterned and should not cause shock or a persistently rigid uterus
workup: Ultrasound when ordered but do not use a normal scan to exclude abruption
management: Maintain IV access and hemorrhage readiness
Prepare for urgent birth when indicated
medicationSafety: Resuscitation and uterotonic/obstetric medications depend on the scenario and orders
Anticoagulant exposure increases bleeding complexity
counselling: Explain that external bleeding may not show the full blood loss
Provide concise support while emergency care proceeds
examTrap: Reassuring the client because only a small amount of vaginal blood is visible.
oneLinePearl: Abruption can bleed inward—pain + rigid uterus + fetal change outranks the pad count.
sourceBasis: Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada guidance/JOGC

title: Umbilical Cord Prolapse
bottomLine: Sudden fetal bradycardia or severe variables after membrane rupture can mean cord prolapse. Call for help, relieve compression, position to reduce pressure, and expedite birth—do not try to push the cord back into the uterus.
recognize: Abrupt fetal bradycardia after rupture of membranes
differentiate: Other fetal heart-rate abnormalities can occur, but cord prolapse after membrane rupture requires immediate exclusion
Maternal hypotension can cause fetal bradycardia without a palpable cord
assessment: Cervical dilation/clinical birth status per team
workup: This is a bedside clinical emergency; do not delay for imaging
management: Manually relieve presenting-part pressure per protocol
medicationSafety: Medication is not the primary fix for mechanical compression
Any tocolytic strategy is team/protocol directed
counselling: Give brief explanations while maintaining pressure relief and emergency focus
followUp: Debrief and support after emergency delivery
examTrap: Attempting to reinsert the cord instead of relieving pressure and preparing for urgent birth.
oneLinePearl: Cord prolapse = lift the presenting part, call for help, get the baby delivered.

title: Uterine Rupture
bottomLine: Prior uterine scar plus sudden pain, fetal bradycardia, loss of station, bleeding, or maternal shock is uterine rupture until proven otherwise. This is an immediate operative emergency.
recognize: Maternal shock may occur with limited vaginal bleeding
differentiate: Abruption also causes pain/fetal compromise but does not typically cause loss of station
Normal labour should not produce shock or abrupt loss of fetal station
assessment: Prior uterine surgery and oxytocin/uterotonic exposure
workup: Immediate obstetric/surgical evaluation; do not delay for nonessential testing
management: Stop uterotonic infusion when directed by protocol/order
medicationSafety: Uterotonics can worsen excessive uterine stimulation
Definitive treatment is surgical; medication does not repair rupture
counselling: Provide brief trauma-informed communication during emergency care
followUp: Postoperative/postpartum and future-pregnancy counselling by obstetric team
examTrap: Waiting for dramatic external bleeding before escalating.
oneLinePearl: Scarred uterus + sudden fetal bradycardia/loss of station = rupture emergency.
sourceBasis: Society of Obstetricians and Gynaecologists of Canada guidance/JOGC

title: Postpartum Endometritis
bottomLine: Postpartum fever with fundal tenderness, lower abdominal pain, and foul lochia suggests uterine infection. Treat promptly and watch for sepsis rather than dismissing fever as normal postpartum recovery.
differentiate: Mastitis localizes to the breast
UTI adds urinary symptoms/flank findings
Normal afterpains should not cause fever/systemic toxicity
medicationSafety: Check allergy and breastfeeding compatibility as appropriate
Do not delay antimicrobials in a deteriorating septic client
counselling: Return for worsening fever, pain, bleeding, or systemic symptoms
followUp: Reassess for retained tissue/abscess if not improving
examTrap: Calling postpartum fever normal without looking for uterine tenderness and systemic deterioration.
oneLinePearl: Postpartum fever + tender uterus + foul lochia = endometritis until assessed.

title: Lactational Mastitis
bottomLine: Mastitis causes a painful inflamed breast with systemic symptoms; breastfeeding or physiologic milk removal usually continues. Worsening systemic illness or a persistent focal mass raises concern for bacterial infection or abscess.
differentiate: Engorgement is usually more diffuse/bilateral without focal inflammatory illness
Abscess causes a persistent/fluctuant collection
Inflammatory breast cancer must be considered when an atypical inflammatory pattern persists
management: Rest, hydration, anti-inflammatory analgesia when safe
Antibiotics when bacterial mastitis is suspected/prescribed
medicationSafety: Review breastfeeding compatibility and allergy
Avoid unnecessary antibiotics for uncomplicated inflammatory symptoms
examTrap: Telling the parent to stop breastfeeding automatically or aggressively massage an inflamed breast.
oneLinePearl: Mastitis: keep milk moving gently; persistent mass or toxicity needs escalation.

title: Wound Dehiscence and Evisceration
bottomLine: Dehiscence is wound separation; evisceration is exposed abdominal viscera. Stop activity, call for urgent surgical help, reduce abdominal strain, cover exposed organs with sterile saline-moistened dressings, keep NPO, and never push organs back in.
differentiate: Superficial skin-edge separation is less severe than fascial failure
Hematoma/infection may precede dehiscence but do not justify probing the wound
workup: CBC/coagulation and other labs as ordered
medicationSafety: Analgesia should not delay assessment
Antibiotics are cause/risk dependent, not a substitute for surgical review
counselling: Explain the need to remain still and avoid straining
followUp: Nutrition, infection, and pressure/strain risk management
examTrap: Trying to reinsert organs or pack the abdomen tightly.
oneLinePearl: Evisceration: moist sterile cover, NPO, urgent surgeon—never push it back.
sourceBasis: Wounds Canada Best Practice Recommendations for Skin Health and Wound Management 2025

title: Skin Tears
bottomLine: Skin tears are traumatic wounds in fragile skin. Clean gently, preserve and realign a viable flap, use atraumatic dressings, and prevent the next tear by reducing friction, shear, and adhesive injury.
differentiate: Skin tear is trauma, not a pressure injury
Purpura/bruising without skin separation is not a tear
workup: Usually clinical wound assessment; investigate deeper injury/infection when indicated
medicationSafety: Anticoagulants can increase bleeding but are not stopped independently
Avoid harsh antiseptics unless specifically indicated
counselling: Use safe transfers/protective clothing as appropriate
examTrap: Cutting off a viable flap or using aggressive adhesive removal.
oneLinePearl: Skin tear = save the flap, protect the skin, prevent more shear.
sourceBasis: Wounds Canada Best Practice Recommendations for Skin Health and Wound Management 2025 — Skin Tears

title: Moisture-Associated Skin Damage
bottomLine: MASD is barrier injury from prolonged moisture/irritants. Fix the moisture source, cleanse gently, protect with an appropriate barrier, and distinguish it from pressure injury because the prevention plan is different.
recognize: Diffuse superficial erythema/erosion in moisture-exposed skin
Irregular edges rather than a classic bony-prominence pressure pattern
differentiate: Pressure injury is driven by pressure/shear and often localizes over pressure points
Candidiasis may produce satellite lesions and needs targeted treatment
workup: Clinical skin assessment; culture/testing only when infection requires it
medicationSafety: Do not use antimicrobials/antifungals without an indication
Avoid products that increase maceration or irritation
redFlags: Mixed pressure/moisture injury needing revised plan
followUp: Reassess skin response and continence/moisture plan
examTrap: Calling every red sacrum a pressure injury without assessing moisture pattern and pressure exposure.
oneLinePearl: MASD: stop the wet, clean gently, barrier the skin, check whether pressure is also involved.
sourceBasis: Wounds Canada Best Practice Recommendations for Skin Health and Wound Management 2025 — MASD

title: Lower-Limb Lymphedema
bottomLine: Lymphedema is chronic protein-rich swelling from impaired lymphatic drainage. Compression/movement and skin care are central when vascular status permits; sudden pain, erythema, fever, or abrupt swelling requires reassessment for cellulitis, DVT, or another acute cause.
recognize: History of lymph-node surgery/radiation, obesity, venous disease, or recurrent cellulitis
differentiate: DVT is an acute thrombotic process
Heart/kidney failure usually produces a different systemic edema pattern
Cellulitis adds erythema, warmth, pain, and systemic symptoms
workup: Vascular testing when compression safety is uncertain
medicationSafety: Diuretics are not a stand-alone cure for lymphatic failure
Antibiotics treat cellulitis, not uncomplicated lymphedema
counselling: Protect skin and treat fungal breaks promptly
examTrap: Applying strong compression to an acutely painful swollen limb without checking for arterial disease or DVT.
oneLinePearl: Chronic lymphedema gets compression and skin care; acute change gets a new diagnosis search.
sourceBasis: Wounds Canada Best Practice Recommendations for Skin Health and Wound Management 2025 — Lymphedema

title: Negative-Pressure Wound Therapy
bottomLine: NPWT depends on a sealed system, patent tubing, prescribed pressure, and close drainage/skin monitoring. Sudden bright-red bleeding, severe new pain, hypotension, or a device alarm with deterioration requires immediate assessment and escalation.
recognize: Sealed dressing connected to controlled suction
differentiate: Air leak/device failure can stop therapy without representing wound infection
Fresh heavy bleeding is not normal exudate
workup: Wound assessment and device troubleshooting per protocol
management: Stop/escalate major bleeding according to emergency protocol
medicationSafety: Anticoagulation increases bleeding risk
Do not simply increase analgesia for unexplained severe new pain without reassessing the wound/device
counselling: Avoid pulling or disconnecting the system
followUp: Review ongoing indication and healing progress
examTrap: Ignoring a high-priority alarm or fresh blood because the pump is still running.
oneLinePearl: NPWT: seal, suction, tubing, drainage—fresh blood is never a routine alarm.
sourceBasis: Wounds Canada Best Practice Recommendations for Skin Health and Wound Management 2025
